r0.name: Fur Brigade
r0.history: The Hudson's Bay Company moved its furs in brigades of boats and pack trains, crewed by voyageurs who knew every portage between the Pacific posts and the bay.

r1.name: Métis Buffalo Hunters
r1.history: The Métis of the Red River organised their great buffalo hunts like a campaign, with captains, scouts and a camp that could form a defensive circle in minutes.

r2.name: Columbia Trappers
r2.history: American free trappers and the first missionaries worked the Columbia basin, which Britain and the United States had agreed in 1818 to occupy jointly.

r3.name: Glengarry Light Infantry
r3.history: Raised in Upper Canada for the War of 1812, the Glengarry Light Infantry Fencibles were remembered as the colony's own regiment when rebellion threatened in 1837.

r4.name: Mountain Men
r4.history: The trappers of the Rocky Mountain fur trade set out from St. Louis each spring for the summer rendezvous, and knew the plains and passes better than any army.

r5.name: Kentucky Riflemen
r5.history: Backcountry militia armed with the long rifle, the men who had held the line at New Orleans in 1815 and who still answered their states' calls.

r6.name: Presidial Cavalry
r6.history: The presidial companies, the soldados de cuera in their layered leather coats, had guarded Mexico's northern frontier since Spanish times.

r7.name: Texas Rangers
r7.history: Formally organised by the Texian provisional government in 1835, the Rangers were mounted volunteers who patrolled the frontier and scouted for the army.

r8.name: Zapadores Battalion
r8.history: The sapper battalion was among the best-trained units of the Mexican army, and led the assault on the Alamo in March 1836.

r9.name: Yucatán Chasseurs
r9.history: Light infantry of the peninsula, raised from a province that resented rule from Mexico City and would declare itself independent in 1841.

r10.name: Morazán's Veterans
r10.history: Francisco Morazán led the Federal Republic of Central America through its civil wars; his veterans knew the highland roads from Guatemala to Costa Rica.

r11.name: Isthmus Militia
r11.history: Panama, a province of New Granada, kept its own militia to guard the crossing between the oceans and the port of Portobelo.

r12.name: Rifles Battalion
r12.history: The Batallón Rifles, first raised with British and Irish volunteers, fought from the Orinoco to Ayacucho in the wars of independence.

r13.name: West India Regiment
r13.history: Britain's West India Regiments, raised from the 1790s, garrisoned the islands and Guiana, where European troops died of fever in their hundreds.

r14.name: Legion of the Guard
r14.history: The Peruvian Legion of the Guard was raised in 1821 and fought at Junín and Ayacucho; Santa Cruz's confederation inherited its traditions.

r15.name: Rio Negro Guard
r15.history: Garrisons of the upper Amazon, holding the river forts against smugglers and the Cabanagem rebels who seized Belém in 1835.

r16.name: Colorados Regiment
r16.history: Bolivia's red-coated guard regiment, the Colorados, formed the core of Santa Cruz's army in his campaign to join Peru and Bolivia.

r17.name: Dragoons of Independence
r17.history: The Imperial Guard of Honour, raised in 1822 to escort Pedro I, whose dragoons rode with him when he proclaimed Brazil's independence.

r18.name: Frontier Dragoons
r18.history: Chile's Dragones de la Frontera held the line of forts along the Biobío, the border with the unconquered Mapuche lands of Araucanía.

r19.name: Colorados del Monte
r19.history: Juan Manuel de Rosas raised the Colorados del Monte from the gauchos of his own estancias in the 1820s; they were the backbone of his rise to power.

r20.name: Rio Grande Lancers
r20.history: The gaúcho horsemen of Rio Grande do Sul were the empire's best cavalry, and in 1835 the core of the Ragamuffin rebellion against it.

r21.name: Gaucho Lancers
r21.history: Horsemen of the pampas, armed with the lance and bolas, who served every faction of the Argentine civil wars.

r22.name: Patagones Garrison
r22.history: The fort at Carmen de Patagones on the Río Negro was the southern limit of Argentine settlement, and beat off a Brazilian landing in 1827.

r23.name: Magellan Strait Watch
r23.history: Lookouts over the strait, where the Beagle's surveys of 1826 to 1834 had charted the channels of Tierra del Fuego.
